This analysis further supported that a reduction in IL-7 availability in the thymus reduces thymocyte proliferation (Figure 2I and J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from pH3 staining and reference to Figures 2I and J.

claims.claim: The thymus of TEC:IL-7HI embryos appeared visibly larger, and the number of pH3 positive cells was significantly increased compared to WT.
claims.source: Compared to WT, the thymus of TEC:IL-7HI embryos appeared visibly larger, and the number of pH3 positive cells was significantly increased (Figure 2I and J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from TEC:IL-7HI embryos and reference to Figures 2I and J.

claims.claim: The in vivo results confirm the critical role of IL-7 for thymocyte proliferation in medaka, a mechanism that is evolutionarily conserved among vertebrates.
claims.source: Therefore, the in vivo results confirm the critical role of IL-7 for thymocyte proliferation in medaka, a mechanism that is evolutionarily conserved among vertebrates (Iwanami et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Iwanami et al., 2011, which discusses the evolutionary conservation of IL-7's role.

claims.claim: The alterations in thymic size suggest a regulatory crosstalk between thymocyte proliferation and TEC architecture.
claims.source: Additionally, the alterations in thymic size suggest a regulatory crosstalk between thymocyte proliferation and TEC architecture.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on an inference from the experimental observations of thymic size changes.

claims.source: Indeed, the scenario with the highest number of thymocytes occurred when signaling deactivation was low and activation was high (274±11, N=4; scenario 45 in Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 3C, which shows the simulation results.

claims.source: Statistical analysis confirms that signal transduction activation aIL-7 and the signal transduction deactivation rate dIL-7 were both statistically significant predictors of thymocyte population size (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1, which shows the statistical analysis results.

claims.claim: There was only a limited reduction in population size with IL-7 depletion (91±11, N=4; scenario 36) compared to no depletion in the reference setting (98±7, N=19).
claims.source: There was only a limited reduction in population size with IL-7 depletion (91±11, N=4; scenario 36 in Figure 3C) compared to no depletion in our reference setting (98±7, N=19).

claims.claim: Introducing a lesioned clone did not markedly alter the division behavior of non-lesioned clones in the same simulation.
claims.source: The clonal analysis of simulations revealed that introducing a lesioned clone did not markedly alter the division behavior of non-lesioned clones in the same simulation (scenario with no lesion: 1.04±1.26 rounds of cell division; scenario with IL7RDA: 0.98±1.22 rounds of cell division; scenario with IL7RHI: 1.04±1.23 rounds of cell division; Figure 4B and C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figures 4B and C, which show the simulation results.

claims.claim: Lesioned clones averaged just above 4 rounds of cell division (4.20±0.34 for IL7RDA and 4.10±0.13 for IL7RHI).
claims.source: In contrast, lesioned clones averaged just above 4 rounds of cell division (4.20±0.34 for IL7RDA and 4.10±0.13 for IL7RHI).

claims.claim: The size of IL7RDA and IL7RHI clones was nearly eightfold larger than an average non-lesioned clone.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 4C, which shows the simulation results.

claims.claim: Lesioned clones acquired a distinct proliferative advantage over non-lesioned clones in the virtual thymus model.
claims.source: This result suggests that lesioned clones acquired a distinct proliferative advantage over non-lesioned clones in our virtual thymus model.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on an inference from the simulation results.

claims.source: Nevertheless, since the expansion of lesioned clones amounted to, at best, only one additional round of cell division compared to the upper range of the non-lesioned clone distribution (Figure 4C), our virtual thymus model predicts that a single lesion in the IL7R gene will not be clinically impactful.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on an inference from the simulation results.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Buffière et al., 2019, which describes ectopic IL-7 expression in malignant T cells.

claims.claim: The lesioned clones consistently showed a higher proliferation rate than their non-lesioned counterpart.
claims.source: The lesioned clones consistently showed a higher proliferation rate than their non-lesioned counterpart (Figure 4E; Figure 4—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 4E and Figure 4—source data 1, which show the simulation results.

claims.claim: Lesioned clones disproportionally gained up to 6 rounds of cell division by modulating proliferative parameters, while normal clones only gained 2 rounds of cell division in the same scenarios.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the text description of the simulation results.

claims.claim: In the scenario with increased proliferation, the first clones to colonize the organ can massively proliferate and completely surround the TECs, preventing later arriving clones from accessing TEC-derived pro-proliferative signals.
claims.source: This difference results from cell crowding creating a disproportional disadvantage to non-lesioned clones: In the scenario with increased proliferation, the first clones to colonize the organ can massively proliferate and completely surround the TECs, preventing later arriving clones from accessing TEC-derived pro-proliferative signals (Figure 4—video 2, right column).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on an inference from the simulation results and reference to Figure 4—video 2.

claims.claim: Lesioned clones carry an intrinsic pro-proliferative advantage due to their lesions in the IL7R, enabling proliferation despite a lack of direct contact with TECs.
claims.source: Thus, these few 'lucky' early colonizers prevent late cells from attaining their full proliferative potential. Lesioned clones carry an intrinsic pro-proliferative advantage due to their lesions in the IL7R, enabling proliferation despite a lack of direct contact with TECs.

claims.claim: Modifying parameters that affected IL-7 activity only enhanced the proliferation rate of non-lesioned clones but showed no impact on either IL7RHI or IL7RDA clones.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 3, which shows the simulation results.

claims.claim: For IL7RHI clones, 10-fold receptor overexpression is enough to activate downstream pro-proliferative effects of the pathway regardless of the parameter permutations tested.
claims.source: While this outcome is expected for IL7RDA clones, which are insensitive to IL-7, for IL7RHI clones, it indicates that 10-fold receptor overexpression is enough to activate downstream pro-proliferative effects of the pathway regardless of the parameter permutations that we tested.

claims.claim: Proliferation of normal clones is strongly affected by IL-7 signaling parameters, gaining up to 3 rounds of cell division between least and most proliferative conditions.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the text description of the simulation results.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 4, which shows the simulation results.

claims.claim: Added IL-7 secretion by lesioned clones with the autocrine lesion had only a small effect on proliferation of non-lesioned clones in the same simulation.
claims.source: Added IL-7 secretion by lesioned clones with the autocrine lesion had only a small effect on proliferation of non-lesioned clones in the same simulation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the text description of the simulation results.

claims.claim: The most critical lesion in conferring a proliferative advantage to lesioned clones was a delay in differentiation.
claims.source: The most critical lesion in conferring a proliferative advantage to lesioned clones was a delay in differentiation.

claims.claim: Identifying a sparse TEC network as a new factor that could influence the clonal expansion of lesioned clones was an unexpected outcome.

results.result: T-ALL represents 10-15% of pediatric and 25% of adult acute lymphoblastic leukemia cases, originates in the thymus, and is characterized by gain-of-function mutations in NOTCH1 (>50% of patients) and IL7R (~10% of patients) genes. These mutations have demonstrated leukemogenic potential across vertebrate models, reflecting evolutionary conservation of thymic developmental mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C8 are well-supported by citations to peer-reviewed literature (Vadillo et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2017; multiple studies for C7; Bajoghli et al., 2019). These claims establish the epidemiological and molecular background for T-ALL and are appropriately referenced to prior work. The statistical data and mechanistic insights are consistent with established knowledge in the field.

results.result: The virtual thymus model simulates individual thymocytes in a spatially resolved computational framework representing 1/10 of a medaka embryonic thymus. The model spans 8.3 days of simulation time (48,000 steps × 15 seconds/step) and reaches homeostasis with ~100 cells, which corresponds to the experimental observation of 877±146 thymocytes at 11 dpf in medaka when scaled appropriately.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C16 describe the computational model setup and validation. The model parameters are clearly defined (C11-C14), and the validation against experimental data (C15-C16) shows good agreement within error margins. The scaling factor (1/10 of organ volume) is explicitly stated and the population dynamics match experimental observations, supporting the model's validity as a representation of medaka thymus development.

results.result: The virtual thymus model implements key biological features: all TECs express Dll4, a subset release IL-7 creating a spatial gradient, ETPs uniformly express Notch1, and IL7R expression varies randomly (0-1) per lineage. The cell cycle averages 7 hours with G1-S-G2-M phases, requires pro-proliferative signals during G1, and stops after differentiation, allowing up to 4 rounds of division. Selection is modeled probabilistically.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C25 describe model implementation details that are consistent with cited prior work (Aghaallaei et al., 2021, 2022) and biological observations (Ruijtenberg and van den Heuvel, 2016 for C22). The model parameters are clearly defined and biologically motivated. The 7-hour cell cycle and up to 4 division rounds are supported by citations and appear reasonable for the system being modeled.

results.result: TEC architecture (size, protrusion number, density) synergistically modulates thymocyte population size. Experimental confocal imaging shows thymocytes occupy 53±3% and TECs 47±3% of thymic area, matching in silico predictions (56±2% and 44±2%). Increasing TEC density, size, and protrusions nearly doubled thymocyte numbers (200±13 vs 98±7 reference), while reducing these parameters halved population size (45±1 to 51±2). Statistical analysis confirmed all three parameters and their interactions significantly predict population size.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C34 present a systematic computational exploration of TEC architecture effects, validated by experimental measurements. The in silico and experimental tissue density measurements are remarkably consistent (C26-C27). The systematic parameter variation (C28-C31) with appropriate replicates (N=3-19) and statistical validation (C32) including interaction effects (C33) provides strong evidence for synergistic effects (C34). The statistical analysis appears rigorous with reference to supplementary figures.

results.result: Spatial distribution of IL-7 critically impacts thymocyte proliferation. When all TECs express IL-7 (scenario 27), population size (155±11) was similar to increased TEC architecture (scenario 26: 200±13), despite higher average IL-7 levels in scenario 27. Spatially restricted IL-7 at the organ periphery (scenario 26) is more effective because thymocytes enter where IL-7 is highest and migrate to IL-7-depleted centers as they become non-proliferative, whereas ubiquitous IL-7 (scenario 27) requires cell migration deeper into the organ before effects manifest.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C42 demonstrate sophisticated spatial modeling revealing that IL-7 distribution pattern matters more than average concentration. The simulation results (C35-C36) are well-documented with appropriate replicates. The mechanistic explanation (C37-C41) is logical and consistent with cited prior work on thymocyte migration patterns (Aghaallaei et al., 2021). This represents an important insight about spatial organization that would be difficult to test experimentally.

results.result: Experimental validation in medaka confirms IL-7's critical role in thymocyte proliferation. IL-7 knockout (il7 crispant) embryos showed fewer thymocytes, smaller thymus size, and reduced pH3+ mitotic cells. Conversely, TEC:IL-7HI embryos with elevated IL-7 had visibly larger thymuses and significantly increased pH3+ cells. These results confirm evolutionary conservation of IL-7's proliferative role and suggest regulatory crosstalk between thymocyte proliferation and TEC architecture.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C47 provide strong experimental validation of computational predictions using CRISPR knockout and overexpression approaches. The use of pH3 as a mitotic marker is appropriate, and the bidirectional manipulation (loss and gain of function) strengthens conclusions. The evolutionary conservation claim (C46) is supported by citation to Iwanami et al., 2011. The inference about TEC-thymocyte crosstalk (C47) is reasonable given the thymic size changes observed.

results.result: IL7R signaling dynamics significantly affect thymocyte population size. High signal activation with low deactivation yielded maximum cells (274±11, scenario 45), while the opposite yielded minimum (42±1, scenario 29). Statistical analysis confirmed both activation and deactivation rates are significant predictors. IL-7 depletion by thymocytes had limited effect (91±11 vs 98±7 reference) and was not statistically significant overall, though effects were more pronounced at higher cell numbers, suggesting self-inhibition via IL-7 depletion occurs only at very high cell densities.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C54 systematically explore IL7R signaling parameters with appropriate statistical analysis. The parameter sweep is well-designed with adequate replicates (N=4-19). Statistical significance is properly assessed (C50, C52) with reference to supplementary figures. The observation that IL-7 depletion effects are density-dependent (C53-C54) is a nuanced finding that demonstrates model sophistication. The inference about self-inhibition (C54) is appropriately cautious.

results.result: Introducing IL7RDA or IL7RHI lesioned clones into simulations showed they acquire proliferative advantage (4.20±0.34 and 4.10±0.13 rounds of division respectively) compared to non-lesioned clones (1.04±1.26 rounds), resulting in nearly eightfold larger clone size. However, this represents only one additional division round compared to the upper range of non-lesioned clones, leading to the prediction that single IL7R lesions alone are not clinically impactful.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C59 introduce lesioned clone modeling with clear quantification. The clonal analysis (C55-C57) shows appropriate statistical reporting with means and standard deviations. The proliferative advantage is well-documented (C58), but the interpretation (C59) that single lesions are insufficient for clinical impact is appropriately conservative given the modest effect size. This sets up the rationale for exploring combinatorial effects in subsequent analyses.

results.result: A systematic computational screen of 1580 scenarios explored combinations of TEC architecture, IL-7 signaling, proliferation parameters, and secondary lesions (reduced motility, autocrine IL-7, delayed differentiation). Lesioned clones consistently showed higher proliferation than non-lesioned counterparts, disproportionally gaining up to 6 rounds of division (vs 2 for normal clones) under increased proliferation conditions. This advantage results from cell crowding: early-arriving lesioned clones can proliferate massively and surround TECs, preventing later non-lesioned clones from accessing pro-proliferative signals, while lesioned clones proliferate despite lacking TEC contact.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C67 describe an extensive systematic exploration with clear documentation of scope (1580 scenarios, C61). The citation supporting autocrine IL-7 production (Buffière et al., 2019, C60) grounds this choice in patient data. The consistent proliferative advantage (C62-C65) is well-documented across multiple parameter combinations. The mechanistic explanation involving cell crowding (C66-C67) is logical and supported by video evidence (Figure 4—video 2), representing an emergent property of the spatial model.

results.result: Modifying IL-7 activity parameters enhanced proliferation of non-lesioned clones (up to 3 rounds of division between extremes) but showed no impact on IL7RHI or IL7RDA clones. For IL7RHI clones, 10-fold receptor overexpression is sufficient to activate downstream pro-proliferative effects regardless of IL-7 parameter permutations tested, while IL7RDA clones are inherently insensitive to IL-7.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70 reveal differential responses to IL-7 signaling modulation between lesioned and non-lesioned clones. The observation that IL7RHI clones are saturated at 10-fold overexpression (C69) is a reasonable inference from the data showing no additional response to IL-7 parameter changes. The contrast with normal clone behavior (C70) strengthens the conclusion that lesioned clones have fundamentally altered signaling dynamics.

results.result: Among secondary lesions tested, delayed differentiation was the most critical for conferring proliferative advantage, essentially doubling the proliferative phase duration and enabling up to 8 rounds of cell division (double that of single IL7R lesions). Reduced cell motility and autocrine IL-7 production showed no added effect when combined with IL7R lesions. This finding aligns with in vivo data implicating differentiation perturbations in cancer initiation and progression.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C75 identify delayed differentiation as the key secondary lesion through systematic testing. The quantitative result (8 vs 4 rounds, C74) is clearly stated. The lack of effect from other lesions (C71-C72) is important negative data. The connection to cancer biology (C75) is appropriately supported by citation (Ruijtenberg and van den Heuvel, 2016), placing findings in broader context. This represents a key mechanistic insight about the importance of differentiation control.

results.result: Unexpectedly, sparse TEC networks amplified lesioned clone expansion while dense TEC networks inhibited it (opposite to non-lesioned clones). Lesioned clones lost 2 rounds of division with increased TEC density while non-lesioned clones gained 2 rounds. The most extreme scenario showed 18 rounds of division in lesioned clones—far exceeding the 12 rounds predicted from additive effects of individual parameter changes—indicating synergistic interactions. At 18 rounds, lesioned clone volume exceeded the simulated organ volume by >1000-fold, suggesting this would cause thymus hyperplasia in vivo, consistent with experimental observations that IL-7 manipulations directly affect organ size.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C84 present a counterintuitive and important finding about TEC density effects. The systematic documentation (C76-C78) with clear quantification (C77, C79) supports the conclusion. The synergistic effect calculation (C79) explicitly shows non-additivity (18 vs 12 predicted rounds). The volume calculation (C81-C82) provides physical context for the biological implications. The experimental validation (C84) strengthens confidence in the prediction. This represents a novel, experimentally-testable prediction about niche-lesion interactions.

results.result: The mechanism underlying sparse TEC benefit for lesioned clones involves NOTCH1 signaling dynamics. In sparse TEC environments, reduced NOTCH1-DLL4 engagement prolongs the undifferentiated proliferative state (turnover time ~80 hr vs <60 hr in dense TECs). While normal clones require both NOTCH1 and IL7R signals for proliferation, lesioned clones with constitutively active IL7R signaling can proliferate without NOTCH1 engagement, thus benefiting from prolonged proliferative windows in sparse TEC conditions. Dense TEC networks promote differentiation, which terminates proliferation in the model.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C93 provide a mechanistic explanation for the sparse TEC advantage through the model's implementation of NOTCH1 signaling. The turnover time measurements (C91) provide quantitative support. The logic is internally consistent with the model structure where NOTCH1 promotes both proliferation and differentiation (incoherent feed-forward loop). The inference that lesioned clones bypass NOTCH1 requirements (C93) follows logically from the constitutive IL7R activation. This represents sophisticated mechanistic insight from the computational model.

results.result: The model implements NOTCH1 signaling as an incoherent feed-forward loop: NOTCH1 promotes proliferation and accelerates differentiation, while differentiation inhibits proliferation. IL7R promotes proliferation independently without affecting differentiation. Simulations predicted that NOTCH1DA lesions alone confer minimal advantage (marginally above high endogenous IL7R), while delayed differentiation lesions substantially increase proliferation. Adding NOTCH1DA to IL7R lesions showed no effect, but combining delayed differentiation with IL7R lesions doubled proliferation, indicating that global NOTCH1 modulation is ineffective due to feedback inhibition, but specifically targeting differentiation enables clonal expansion.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C102 describe the NOTCH1 signaling implementation and its effects on lesioned clones. The incoherent feed-forward loop structure (C95) is well-established in biology and appropriately cited (Aghaallaei et al., 2021). The simulation results (C97-C100) clearly distinguish between global NOTCH1 activation (ineffective) and differentiation-specific effects (effective). The mechanistic interpretation about feedback inhibition (C101) is reasonable given the model structure. This sets up important predictions for experimental validation.

results.result: Experimental validation in medaka showed that NICD∆PEST alone (N=32) did not cause thymus hyperplasia at 11 dpf, supporting the model prediction that NOTCH1 activation alone is insufficient within 8 days. However, combining NICD∆PEST with mycn resulted in 25% thymus hyperplasia (N=36), with 8% showing T-ALL with organ infiltration. Analysis revealed ectopic il7 expression in transformed thymocytes while endogenous il7r remained unchanged. MYCN, a downstream effector of NOTCH1 in thymocytes, likely shifts the proliferation-differentiation balance toward proliferation, and transformed cells acquire autocrine IL-7 production capability.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C110 provide strong experimental validation with appropriate sample sizes and clear phenotypic criteria. The negative result with NICD∆PEST alone (C103) validates the model prediction. The positive result with NICD∆PEST+mycn (C104-C105) demonstrates the importance of downstream effectors. The molecular analysis (C106-C107) using FACS sorting and qPCR/WISH provides mechanistic insight. The interpretation about MYCN's role (C108-C109) is well-supported by citations. The autocrine IL-7 finding (C110) represents an important emergent property of transformation.

results.result: IL7R overexpression experiments showed thymus hyperplasia in 26% (il7r, N=49) or 59% (il7rNPC, N=29) of embryos. The il7rNPC condition showed significant lck upregulation compared to WT, while il7rHI did not. Combining il7rNPC with NICD∆PEST and mycn yielded 73% thymus hyperplasia (N=33) with 33% showing T-ALL phenotype, suggesting additive effects. GFP/pH3 double staining confirmed increased mitotic cells in thymuses, notably in the inner zone where WT thymocytes are normally quiescent, indicating ectopic proliferation in differentiated compartments.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C118 demonstrate dose-dependent and combinatorial effects of IL7R manipulations with appropriate sample sizes. The differential lck upregulation (C113-C114) suggests il7rNPC is more potently activating than simple overexpression. The high frequency of hyperplasia/T-ALL with triple manipulation (C115-C116) supports synergistic effects. The pH3 staining in the inner zone (C118) with appropriate citations (Bajoghli et al., 2015, 2021) demonstrates spatial disruption of normal proliferation patterns, representing strong phenotypic evidence.

results.result: The model prediction that NOTCH1 activation alone doesn't increase proliferation (due to incoherent feed-forward loop triggering differentiation) was validated experimentally: NOTCH1 activation alone showed no hyperplasia within 8 days, but combining with mycn did. However, this contrasts with other systems where long-term NOTCH1 activation (weeks in zebrafish, months in mice) drives T-ALL. Possible explanations for this discrepancy include: different proliferation-differentiation balance in vivo than modeled, additional negative feedbacks not considered, proliferation continuing past differentiation with sufficient NOTCH1 stimulation, or long-term misregulation promoting additional compounding lesions.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C129 identify an important discrepancy between the model/short-term experiments and long-term in vivo studies. The experimental validation (C120-C121) supports the model within the 8-day window. The citations to long-term studies (C122-C123) are appropriate. However, the proposed explanations (C126-C129) are speculative without additional data. The 8-day timeframe limitation (C124) is acknowledged but doesn't fully resolve the discrepancy. The model's inability to produce hyperplasia with NOTCH1 alone regardless of duration (C125) suggests a fundamental limitation that requires further investigation.

results.result: In vivo results support computational predictions: IL7R overexpression alone, but not NOTCH1 alone, induces thymus hyperplasia rapidly. Dual activation of IL7R and the NOTCH1-MYCN axis promotes clonal expansion in vivo, leading to rapid thymus hyperplasia and T-ALL development in medaka within 8 days.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C131 summarize the key experimental findings that validate major model predictions. The differential effects of IL7R vs NOTCH1 manipulation (C130) are clearly demonstrated across multiple experiments. The rapid T-ALL development within 8 days (C131) is remarkable and well-documented with appropriate sample sizes and phenotypic criteria. This represents strong validation of the model's predictive power for combinatorial effects.

results.result: When all TECs express IL-7 (scenario 27), lesioned clones with IL7RHI or extended differentiation showed significant clonal expansion advantage. Experimentally, TEC:IL-7HI embryos showed 12% thymus hyperplasia (N=24) without organ infiltration. Co-injecting il7 overexpression in TECs with il7r in thymocytes increased hyperplasia to 41% (N=32). Combining TEC il7 overexpression with thymocyte NICD and mycn showed synergistic effects, with 25% developing T-ALL (N=48). These results demonstrate that excess thymic IL-7 combined with alterations affecting thymocyte differentiation triggers rapid T-ALL development.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C138 systematically test the role of niche-derived IL-7 in disease progression. The computational prediction (C132) is validated experimentally with appropriate controls and sample sizes (C133-C137). The progression from single manipulations (12%, 41%) to combined manipulations (25% T-ALL) demonstrates clear synergy. The conclusion (C138) appropriately integrates computational and experimental findings. This represents a key insight about niche-tumor interactions that challenges gene-centric views of T-ALL.

results.result: Experimental observations suggest additional negative feedback from pro-proliferative signaling to differentiation not included in the model. Manipulations in IL7R or thymic IL-7 levels alone are sufficient to induce hyperplasia and T-ALL in vivo—more severe than model predictions. In simulations, massive overproliferation required modifying multiple parameters (delayed differentiation, accelerated divisions, reduced TEC density) because differentiation is a hard stop to proliferation regardless of pro-proliferative stimuli. The authors propose that continued thymocyte proliferation can downregulate differentiation pathways, maintaining cells in a constant proliferative state—a negative feedback loop from proliferation to differentiation that could explain model-experiment discrepancies.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C145 identify an important limitation of the current model. The observation that experimental effects exceed predictions (C140-C141) is well-documented. The model constraint (C142) is clearly stated. However, the proposed negative feedback mechanism (C144-C145) is speculative without direct experimental evidence. While the hypothesis is reasonable and could explain discrepancies, it requires additional experiments to test. The authors appropriately acknowledge this as a limitation and propose a testable mechanism for future work.

results.result: This study demonstrates synergy between computational modeling and in vivo validation for dissecting organ-level disease mechanisms, highlighting the previously underexplored role of TECs and thymic niche in T-ALL development. Through >1500 simulated scenarios, the study identified TEC network alterations (shape, density, spatial organization) as drivers—factors difficult to manipulate experimentally. In vivo results confirmed that enriched thymic IL-7 accelerates disease progression, especially with enhanced IL7R or constitutively active NOTCH1/MYCN. These findings challenge the gene-centric T-ALL paradigm and emphasize the critical influence of thymic microenvironment spatial structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C146-C150 provide appropriate summary and contextualization of the study's contributions. The methodological integration (C146) is well-demonstrated throughout. The novelty regarding TEC/niche roles (C147) is justified given the focus on cell-autonomous factors in prior T-ALL research. The computational scope (C148) is accurately stated. The experimental validation (C149) is well-documented. The paradigm challenge (C150) is appropriate given the demonstrated importance of spatial niche structure. These summary claims accurately reflect the major findings.

results.result: The model has several limitations: it was calibrated for medaka embryonic thymus and may not fully capture dynamics of other species (particularly human); it cannot represent TEC shape changes over time or TEC proliferation due to treating particles as loose objects; it simplifies T-cell developmental stages by not considering IL-7/Notch cross-regulatory feedback loops or thymic growth over time. These simplifications stem from lack of species-specific knowledge and tools in medaka. Adapting the framework for murine or human contexts with well-characterized markers and emerging TEC architecture data could enable exploration of these questions.
results.evaluation: Claims C151-C155 provide honest assessment of model limitations. The species-specificity concern (C151) is valid and appropriately cited. The technical limitations (C152) are clearly explained with mechanistic reasoning. The biological simplifications (C153) are acknowledged with appropriate justification (C154). The forward-looking statement (C155) with citation to emerging work (Lagou et al., 2024) is reasonable. This transparent discussion of limitations strengthens confidence in the work by showing the authors understand the model's scope and boundaries.

results.result: Despite current simplifications, the integrative approach offers valuable insights into how microenvironmental factors influence leukemia expansion and provides a framework for exploring their role in chemoresistance and relapse. These findings open avenues for developing therapeutic strategies targeting the leukemic-supportive niche to potentially improve T-ALL treatment outcomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C156-C157 appropriately contextualize the study's translational potential while acknowledging limitations. The framework's value (C156) is supported by the demonstrated ability to generate testable predictions about niche-tumor interactions. The therapeutic implications (C157) are appropriately cautious ('open avenues', 'potential') given that this is basic research. These forward-looking statements are reasonable extensions of the findings without overstating clinical applicability.

results.result: The authors developed a virtual thymus computational model that simulates individual thymocytes and TECs in a spatially resolved environment, calibrated to reproduce medaka embryonic thymus dynamics over approximately 8.3 days, reaching a homeostatic population of ~100 cells that matches experimental observations when scaled appropriately.
results.evaluation: All reviewers acknowledge and accept the computational model as a key strength of the study. Reviewer 1 states 'the modelling yields some interesting and solid findings,' Reviewer 2 notes 'the strength of the paper is the use of computational modelling to obtain unique insights,' and Reviewer 3 highlights 'attractive features of the computational model are stochasticity, cell-to-cell variability, and spatial heterogeneity.' No concerns are raised about the model's basic implementation or calibration.

results.result: Computational simulations across 26 scenarios predict that TEC network architecture (size, protrusion number, and density) synergistically modulates thymocyte population size, with denser/larger TECs increasing populations nearly twofold (scenario 26: 200±13 cells) and sparse/smaller TECs reducing populations by half (scenarios 1 and 6: 45±1 and 51±2 cells respectively) compared to reference conditions (98±7 cells).
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly recognize this as a key finding. Reviewer 1 states the modeling 'demonstrated that increasing TEC size, density, or protrusions increased the number of thymocytes,' and Reviewer 2 notes the model provides 'unique insights into the niche parameters that control T cell development, such as the role of TEC architecture.' No concerns are raised about these computational predictions.

results.result: Simulations reveal that spatially restricted IL-7 at the thymic periphery (scenario 26) is more effective at driving population growth than ubiquitous IL-7 expression (scenario 27), despite lower average extracellular IL-7 levels, due to the spatial organization of thymocyte entry and migration patterns within the thymic niche.
results.evaluation: This spatial finding is implicitly accepted by reviewers as part of the overall computational results. Reviewer 2 specifically notes 'the role of TEC architecture' as a strength, and no reviewer questions the spatial dynamics predictions. The finding is treated as a natural extension of the model's capabilities.

results.result: In vivo validation in medaka shows that il7 crispant embryos have fewer thymocytes and smaller thymus size with reduced proliferation, while TEC:IL-7HI embryos show larger thymus and increased pH3-positive cells, confirming IL-7's critical role in thymocyte proliferation and suggesting crosstalk between thymocyte proliferation and TEC architecture.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge these experimental validations. Reviewer 3 states 'there are some experimental results in Figures 4,5 and 6. For example, il7 crispant embryos have fewer thymocytes and smaller thymii; but increasing IL-7 availability produces large thymii.' Reviewer 2 notes the study 'anchor[s] those findings with in vivo experiments.' The experimental support for IL-7's role is accepted without challenge.

results.result: Systematic variation of IL-7 signaling parameters (activation and deactivation rates) shows these are statistically significant predictors of thymocyte population size, though IL-7 depletion by thymocytes has minimal effect except at very high cell numbers, suggesting self-inhibition via IL-7 depletion is limited under normal conditions.
results.evaluation: These computational parameter explorations are implicitly accepted as part of the systematic modeling approach. Reviewer 3 notes the model 'tested the effects of varying a few key parameters of cell proliferation,' and no concerns are raised about the IL-7 signaling dynamics predictions.

results.result: Simulations with lesioned clones (IL7RDA or IL7RHI) show these clones undergo ~4 rounds of division versus ~1 for normal clones, resulting in nearly eightfold larger clone sizes, though the model predicts a single IL7R lesion will not be clinically impactful as it provides only one additional division round compared to the upper range of normal clones.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly describes this finding: 'ordinary clones have IL7R levels chosen from a distribution, while lesioned clones have an IL7R value set to the maximum. The observation is that the lesioned clones are larger families, but the difference is not dramatic.' This characterization aligns with the authors' interpretation that single lesions have limited impact.

results.result: Systematic exploration of 1580 scenarios reveals that lesioned clones consistently show higher proliferation than non-lesioned clones across parameter variations, gaining up to 6 rounds of division (versus 2 for normal clones) when proliferative parameters are modulated, with cell crowding creating disproportionate disadvantages for non-lesioned clones by blocking TEC access.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly recognizes this mechanism: 'One promising cell-extrinsic mechanism is mentioned: if a lesioned clone happens to be near a source of IL-7 and begins to proliferate, the progeny can crowd out cells of other clones and monopolise the IL-7 source.' This crowding effect is accepted as a key finding from the systematic simulations.

results.result: Among secondary lesions tested, delayed differentiation is the most critical for conferring proliferative advantage, essentially doubling the proliferative phase duration and enabling up to 8 rounds of cell division (double that of single IL7R lesions), consistent with in vivo data implicating differentiation perturbations in cancer initiation.
results.evaluation: This finding is implicitly accepted as part of the systematic parameter exploration. Reviewers acknowledge the comprehensive testing of parameters (Reviewer 3: 'tested the effects of varying a few key parameters'), and no concerns are raised about the differentiation delay predictions.

results.result: Unexpectedly, sparse TEC networks amplify lesioned clone expansion (while disadvantaging normal clones), with parameter combinations of reduced TEC density and size overrepresented in scenarios showing maximal proliferation (up to 18 rounds of division), suggesting a defective niche synergistically amplifies pro-proliferative modulations and could lead to thymus hyperplasia in vivo.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly highlights this finding: 'The effect will be more noticeable if sources are rare, so is seen when the TEC network is sparse.' Reviewer 4 identifies this as 'One key finding is that a dense TEC network inhibits the proliferation of malignant cells and favors the proliferation of normal cells, whereas a sparse TEC network leads to rapid expansion of malignant thymocytes.' This is recognized as a novel and important discovery.

results.result: The model predicts that reduced TEC density decreases NOTCH1-DLL4 engagement, prolonging the undifferentiated proliferative phase (turnover time ~80 hr with sparse TECs versus <60 hr with dense TECs), which benefits lesioned clones with intrinsically high IL7R signaling that can proliferate without Notch signaling.
results.evaluation: This mechanistic explanation for the sparse TEC effect is implicitly accepted as part of the model's logic. Reviewers do not challenge the NOTCH1-differentiation dynamics, and Reviewer 3's acknowledgment of the sparse TEC effect implies acceptance of the underlying mechanism.

results.result: Simulations predict that NOTCH1DA modification alone provides minimal proliferative advantage (only marginally higher than high endogenous IL7R), while delayed differentiation leads to higher proliferation; combining NOTCH1DA with IL7R lesions shows no added effect, but combining delayed differentiation with IL7R lesions doubles proliferation, indicating global NOTCH1 modulation is ineffective due to feedback inhibition.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly notes 'Critical outcomes from the computational model were tested in vivo using medaka fish, such as the role of IL-7 signalling and minimal effect of Notch signalling.' This characterization aligns with the model's prediction that NOTCH1 activation alone has minimal impact.

results.result: In vivo experiments show that NICDΔPEST alone does not cause thymus hyperplasia (0/32 embryos), but combining NICDΔPEST with mycn results in 25% hyperplasia (9/36 embryos) with 8% showing T-ALL phenotype and massive organ infiltration; analysis reveals ectopic il7 expression in transformed thymocytes, suggesting MYCN shifts the NOTCH1 feed-forward loop balance toward proliferation.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly acknowledges 'Critical outcomes from the computational model were tested in vivo using medaka fish, such as... minimal effect of Notch signalling.' The experimental validation that NOTCH1 alone is insufficient is accepted, as is the synergistic effect with MYCN.

results.result: IL7R overexpression alone induces thymus hyperplasia in 26% (il7r) or 59% (il7rNPC) of embryos, with il7rNPC showing significant lck upregulation; combining il7rNPC with NICDΔPEST and mycn yields 73% hyperplasia frequency with 33% showing T-ALL phenotype, increased mitotic cells, and pH3-positive cells in normally quiescent thymic zones.
results.evaluation: These experimental results are implicitly accepted by reviewers as part of the in vivo validation. Reviewer 2 notes the study 'anchor[s] those findings with in vivo experiments,' and no concerns are raised about the IL7R overexpression experiments or their outcomes.

results.result: In vivo results support simulations showing IL7R overexpression alone (but not NOTCH1 alone) induces thymus hyperplasia rapidly, while dual activation of IL7R and NOTCH1-MYCN axis promotes rapid T-ALL development within 8 days in medaka; the lack of hyperplasia with NOTCH1 alone may reflect the shorter 8-day timeframe versus weeks/months required in other systems, or model limitations in representing NOTCH1's proliferative effects.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states this as a key validated outcome: 'Critical outcomes from the computational model were tested in vivo using medaka fish, such as the role of IL-7 signalling and minimal effect of Notch signalling.' The agreement between model predictions and experimental results is recognized as a strength.

results.result: In IL-7-enriched thymic environments (all TECs expressing IL-7), lesioned clones show significant clonal expansion advantage; in vivo, TEC:IL-7HI embryos show 12% hyperplasia, increasing to 41% when combined with il7r overexpression in thymocytes, and 25% T-ALL frequency when combined with NICD and mycn, revealing that excess thymic IL-7 combined with differentiation alterations triggers rapid T-ALL development.
results.evaluation: These experimental results are implicitly accepted as part of the comprehensive in vivo validation. Reviewer 3 notes 'increasing IL-7 availability produces large thymii,' and the synergistic effects with other manipulations are not questioned by any reviewer.

results.result: Experimental observations suggest additional negative feedback from pro-proliferative signaling to differentiation beyond what the model includes; manipulations in IL7R or thymic IL-7 levels induce more severe hyperplasia/T-ALL than model predictions, and NOTCH1-MYCN upregulation suggests proliferation can proceed unbridled by differentiation when sufficiently stimulated, leading to the proposal that continued proliferation can downregulate differentiation pathways.
results.evaluation: While reviewers accept the experimental findings, they do not explicitly evaluate the proposed negative feedback mechanism or the discrepancy between model predictions and experimental severity. The authors acknowledge this as a model limitation and propose a hypothesis, but reviewers do not comment on whether this explanation is convincing or requires further validation.

results.result: The study demonstrates synergy between computational modeling and experimental validation in dissecting thymic niche contributions to T-ALL, highlighting the previously underexplored role of TECs and identifying TEC network architecture alterations as drivers of disease; results challenge the gene-centric T-ALL paradigm by emphasizing the thymic microenvironment's spatial structure.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly recognize this as the study's major contribution. Reviewer 1 calls it 'important,' Reviewer 2 states 'the strength of the paper is the use of computational modelling to obtain unique insights,' Reviewer 3 notes the ability to 'follow cell lineages,' and Reviewer 4 highlights 'A key strength of this study is that it combines computational modeling using an agent-based model with experimental work.'

results.result: The authors acknowledge model limitations including calibration to medaka (not human), inability to represent TEC shape changes or proliferation, lack of cross-regulatory feedback loops between IL-7 and Notch pathways, and absence of thymic growth over time; they propose adapting the framework to murine/human contexts and suggest the approach offers insights for developing therapeutic strategies targeting the leukemic-supportive niche.
results.evaluation: Reviewers implicitly accept these limitations as reasonable for the current study. Reviewer 2 states 'I can't comment on the model itself, as I am not an expert in modelling, however, the conclusions of the paper seem to be well-supported by the model,' suggesting the limitations do not undermine the main findings. No reviewer challenges the proposed future directions.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate the computational model setup and validation (C9-C16). OpenEval provides detailed technical assessment of model parameters and validation metrics, while peer reviewers broadly accept the model as a key strength without raising concerns about implementation or calibration. Peer R1 also covers model implementation details (C17-C27) that OpenEval addresses separately in R3-R4.

Both address model implementation details (C17-C25). OpenEval provides detailed evaluation of biological motivation and parameter choices with citations, while peer reviewers accept these as part of the overall model framework, noting attractive features like stochasticity and spatial heterogeneity.

Both evaluate TEC architecture effects (C28-C34). OpenEval emphasizes systematic parameter variation, statistical rigor, and synergistic effects. Peer reviewers explicitly recognize this as a key finding demonstrating unique insights into niche parameters controlling T cell development. Complete agreement on the validity and importance of these results.

Perfect claim overlap (C35-C42) on IL-7 spatial distribution findings. Both evaluations support the conclusion that IL-7 distribution pattern matters more than average concentration. OpenEval highlights this as sophisticated spatial modeling with mechanistic explanation; peer reviewers implicitly accept it as part of TEC architecture insights.

Both evaluate experimental validation of IL-7 role (C43-C47, with peer R4 also covering C84).
